title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 31–32 (editorial review pending approval)
description: Editorial review of Units 31–32: animals and travelling, including illustrated vocabulary, exercise contexts, British English pronunciation, Portuguese translations, and original English examples. Human and browser release checks remain outstanding.
sourceNotice: Learning targets and coverage were checked against the user-supplied textbook, printed pages 68–71. Example sentences and usage notes are original; textbook images and exercises are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, animal-product table, illustrations, captions, common mistakes and exercises 31.1–31.5 and 32.1–32.4 were inspected. Provenance is identified at item level.

audit.cannotGuarantee: Coverage reflects the inspected teaching material and exercise targets, not a reproduction of every activity. Real browser import, text-to-speech and backup/restore tests have not been executed.

units.title: Unit 31 — Animals
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition), Unit 31, textbook pp. 68–69 (PDF pp. 69–70); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: Every animal on the farm needs fresh water.
items.note: A general word. This unit groups animals into farm animals, wild or zoo animals, and pets.

items.example: The brown horse is standing near the gate.
items.note: The source table associates horses with hair and meat. A young horse is a foal.

items.example: The farmer has three cows in the field.
items.note: A young cow is a calf. Cows provide milk and can also be a source of leather and beef.

items.example: There are six sheep near the fence.
items.note: The singular and plural are the same: one sheep, two sheep. Sheep provide wool and meat (lamb).

items.example: A pink pig is sleeping beside the barn.
items.note: A young pig is a piglet. Pork, bacon and ham are names of meat or meat products from pigs.

items.pt: galinha ou frango; carne de frango
items.example: The chickens are looking for food.
items.note: Chicken refers to the bird or its meat. Hen specifically means an adult female chicken.

items.example: One hen is sitting beside the other birds.
items.note: A hen is an adult female chicken; a chick is a young bird. Hen and chicken are not always interchangeable.

items.example: The goat is eating grass behind the house.
items.note: A young goat is a kid. Goat can refer to a male or female animal.

items.example: A sheep is a common farm animal.
items.note: A farm animal is an animal kept on a farm, such as a cow, pig or sheep.

items.example: The young foal stays close to its mother.
items.note: A young horse; compare calf, which is a young cow.

items.example: The calf is drinking water beside the cow.
items.note: A young cow. The irregular plural is calves /kɑːvz/.

items.example: They have a new lamb on the farm.
items.note: A lamb is a young sheep; lamb also refers to its meat. The final b is silent.

items.example: A tiny piglet ran across the yard.
items.note: A young pig.

items.example: The chick followed the hen around the garden.
items.note: A young bird, especially a young chicken. Chick and chicken do not always have the same meaning.

items.example: The goat and her kid slept in the barn.
items.note: Here kid means a young goat. In informal English, a kid can also mean a child.

items.example: We buy fresh milk from a local farm.
items.note: The source associates milk with cows and goats. Milk is normally an uncountable noun.

items.example: These boots are made of leather.
items.note: Material made from animal hide, used for shoes, clothing and bags. Do not confuse it with wool.

items.example: This jumper is made from sheep’s wool.
items.note: Sheep produce wool, which is used to make clothes and other textiles.

items.example: The brush is made with horse hair.
items.note: The source lists hair as a product of horses; hair can also refer to the hair on a person's head.

items.example: The shop sells different types of meat.
items.note: A general noun. Beef, pork, lamb and chicken name particular types of meat.

items.example: We bought some beef for dinner.
items.note: Cow is an animal; beef is the meat from cattle.

items.example: This restaurant does not serve pork.
items.note: Pig is an animal; pork is meat from pigs.

items.example: He had some bacon with his breakfast.
items.note: Bacon is a meat product from pigs, usually cured, and is not a general synonym for pork.

items.example: She made a sandwich with cheese and ham.
items.note: Ham is a meat product from pigs; pork is the broader name for pig meat.

items.example: There is an egg in the bowl.
items.note: Hens lay eggs. The plural is eggs.

items.example: This farm sells fresh produce in the local market.
items.note: In the farm-animal table, produce is a noun meaning things supplied by farms or animals. The verb produce /prəˈdʒuːs/ has stress on the second syllable.

items.example: An elephant walked slowly towards the river.
items.note: A large wild animal also shown in the picture-identification exercises.

items.example: A monkey climbed up the tree.
items.note: The plural is monkeys, not monkies.

items.example: The tiger is resting in the shade.
items.note: Tigers and lions are large wild cats, not farm animals.

items.example: We saw a lion sleeping at the zoo.
items.note: A meat-eating wild animal; the exercises identify lions and tigers as large cats.

items.example: The giraffe can reach the leaves high in the tree.
items.note: The exercises identify a giraffe by its very long neck.

items.example: A snake was lying on a warm rock.
items.note: A general word for these reptiles; not every snake is venomous.

items.example: A lion is a wild animal.
items.note: A wild animal normally lives in nature rather than being domesticated.

items.example: We visited the zoo during our holiday.
items.note: A place where people can see animals, including many wild animals.

items.example: Our family has one small pet.
items.note: A pet is an animal kept at home for companionship. Do you have any pets? asks about pets in general.

items.example: We have two fish in a small tank.
items.note: Fish is usually both singular and plural. Fishes is also possible when talking about different species.

items.example: The rabbit jumped across the grass.
items.note: The exercises associate rabbits with hopping and jumping.

items.example: Our cat likes sleeping on the sofa.
items.note: Cats can be pets; compare wild cats such as lions and tigers.

items.example: Her dog waits by the door every morning.
items.note: For the everyday activity, say take a dog for a walk.

items.example: The colourful parrot sat on a branch.
items.note: A parrot is a bird, a category also used in the exercises.

items.example: The tortoise moves slowly around the garden.
items.note: A tortoise lives mainly on land; turtle often refers to an aquatic animal. The exercise mentions a tortoise sleeping in winter.

items.example: A parrot is a colourful bird.
items.note: Parrots, hens and chickens are birds.

items.word: take a dog for a walk
items.example: I take my dog for a walk after work.
items.note: Use take + an animal or person + for a walk. The expression means walking with them, not simply picking them up.

items.pt: alimentar um animal; dar comida a um animal
items.example: Please feed the animals before you leave.
items.note: Feed is irregular: feed – fed – fed.

items.example: Remember to give the rabbit clean water.
items.note: The pattern is give + animal + water. You can also say give water to the animal.

items.example: Do you have a pet at home?
items.note: A common question is Do you have any pets? Use the plural after any in this question.

items.pt: andar a cavalo; montar um cavalo
items.example: My cousin is learning to ride a horse.
items.note: Ride means to sit on and control an animal or vehicle. Its past and past participle are rode and ridden.

learningObjectives: Identify the illustrated animals and group them as farm animals, wild or zoo animals, or pets.
Match farm animals to their young and products, including horse/foal, cow/calf, sheep/lamb, pig/piglet, hen/chick and goat/kid.
Distinguish animal names from meat names (beef, pork, lamb and chicken) and recognise leather, wool, hair, bacon and ham.
Use sheep for both singular and plural, and distinguish chicken from hen and kid from child.
Describe animal care using feed, give water and take a dog for a walk; use ride a horse correctly.
Recognise birds, large cats and jumping animals from descriptions in the exercises.

units.title: Unit 32 — Travelling
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition), Unit 32, textbook pp. 70–71 (PDF pp. 71–72); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: Public transport is useful in big cities.
items.note: Types of transport include land, air and water transport.

items.example: We travelled to the next city by train.
items.note: For the mode of transport, use by train without an article.

items.example: The bus stops outside the hospital.
items.note: When giving directions, say take a bus or take the bus.

items.example: My sister rides her bicycle to college.
items.note: Bike is a shorter, more informal word for bicycle.

items.example: He bought a new bike last month.
items.note: Usually means bicycle; in some contexts bike can also mean motorbike.

items.example: We took a taxi back to the hotel.
items.note: A common combination is take a taxi.

items.example: An aeroplane flew above our town.
items.note: Aeroplane is British spelling; airplane is American spelling. Plane is common in both.

items.example: Our plane arrived early this morning.
items.note: A shorter form of aeroplane, common in speech and writing.

items.example: They drove their car to the coast.
items.note: The unit teaches hire a car, fill it up with petrol and give someone a lift.

items.example: A helicopter flew over the mountains.
items.note: A type of aircraft with rotating blades; unlike an aeroplane, it can usually take off vertically.

items.example: He goes to work on his motorbike.
items.note: Another common word for motorcycle.

items.example: Her motorcycle is parked near the office.
items.note: Also called a motorbike; do not confuse it with a bicycle.

items.example: We went across London on the underground.
items.note: In London, the underground is also called the Tube. Other cities may use metro or subway.

items.example: The small boat crossed the lake.
items.note: Boat usually refers to a smaller watercraft than ship, though usage varies.

items.example: A large ship entered the harbour.
items.note: Ship usually refers to a large vessel, often larger than a boat.

items.example: I checked the map before leaving the station.
items.note: A map helps you plan routes and give directions.

items.pt: quadro de horários; tabela de horários
items.example: The timetable shows the next train at nine.
items.note: Shows departure and arrival times; a timetable is not a ticket.

items.example: They asked a question at customs.
items.note: In this meaning, the word ends in -s. Customs is not the same as custom, meaning a tradition.

items.example: Our luggage is still at the airport.
items.note: Normally uncountable: say some luggage or two bags, not a luggage or luggages.

items.example: She put her passport in her jacket pocket.
items.note: The normal expression for examining this document is check someone's passport.

items.example: Keep your ticket until the end of the journey.
items.note: Single tickets and return tickets are two types of travel ticket.

items.example: I need a single ticket to Bristol.
items.note: A single ticket covers one journey to a destination, not the return journey.

items.example: She bought a return ticket to Brighton.
items.note: A return ticket covers both outward and return journeys; in American English, round-trip ticket is common.

items.pt: reservar um assento; reservar um lugar
items.example: We booked two seats for the evening train.
items.note: Here book is a verb meaning reserve, not the noun book. You can also say reserve a seat.

items.example: Please reserve a seat before Friday.
items.note: Reserve and book are alternatives when arranging a seat for a journey.

items.example: Buy the tickets in advance to avoid problems.
items.note: The whole expression is in advance, meaning before the expected time.

items.example: The journey from the airport took forty minutes.
items.note: Use journey for a particular trip from one place to another: Was the journey long? not Was the travel long?

items.example: I travel by train when I can.
items.note: Travel commonly functions as a verb or a broad uncountable noun; journey refers to one particular trip.

items.example: Is this seat free?
items.note: To book or reserve a seat is to arrange a place to sit; it does not just mean buying a ticket.

items.example: Our train leaves from platform five.
items.note: The part of a railway station where passengers wait for or board trains.

items.example: The morning train arrives at seven.
items.note: Say arrive at a station and arrive in a city. Do not normally use arrive to for a destination.

items.example: The train departs from platform two.
items.note: More formal than leave in announcements. Trains depart from a platform.

items.example: Our train leaves in ten minutes.
items.note: Irregular verb: leave – left – left. Depart is a more formal alternative for services.

items.example: We had lunch in the restaurant car.
items.note: A carriage on a train where passengers can buy meals.

items.example: You have to change trains at Oxford.
items.note: Say change trains without an article. You can also change at a station.

items.example: There is a direct train to the airport.
items.note: A direct train takes you to your destination without needing to change trains.

items.example: Get off the train at the next stop.
items.note: Get off a train or bus; usually get out of a car or taxi.

items.example: We got on the bus outside the station.
items.note: Get on a bus, train or plane. The opposite is get off.

items.example: Meet me outside the railway station.
items.note: Used in the travel-directions exercise when changing between buses, trains and taxis.

items.example: We got off at the last stop.
items.note: The point where you leave a vehicle. A bus stop is not the same as a railway station.

items.example: We arrived at the airport very early.
items.note: Say at the airport. You normally check in before boarding a flight.

items.example: We checked in at the airport two hours before our flight.
items.note: Check in is the verb phrase; check-in is the noun or adjective.

items.example: Online check-in was available the day before our flight.
items.note: Online check-in is a noun phrase. The corresponding verb phrase is check in online.

items.example: The plane took off just after midday.
items.note: An aircraft takes off when it leaves the ground. The past form is took off.

items.example: Keep your boarding card ready at the gate.
items.note: A document for boarding a flight, different from a passport or travel ticket. Boarding pass is also common.

items.example: A flight attendant helped the passenger.
items.note: A member of the crew who looks after passengers on an aircraft.

items.example: Our flight was comfortable and quiet.
items.note: Have a good flight! is a way of wishing someone well before an air journey.

items.pt: tenha um bom voo; boa viagem (de avião)
items.example: Have a good flight and call us when you arrive!
items.note: A friendly expression used when someone is about to travel by plane.

items.example: Our plane landed in Madrid at midnight.
items.note: Opposite of take off for an aircraft. The regular past form is landed.

items.example: The landing was smooth despite the wind.
items.note: A noun derived from land: after landing means after the plane has arrived on the ground.

items.example: We went through customs after collecting our bags.
items.note: The expression is go through customs. Passport control and customs checks are different procedures.

items.example: An officer checked my passport at the airport.
items.note: Say check a passport, not control a passport, when you mean inspect the document.

items.example: We hired a car for four days.
items.note: Hire means rent temporarily in this context; buying a car means purchasing it.

items.example: We filled the car up with petrol before returning it.
items.note: Use fill + vehicle + up with petrol. Petrol is the British English word for gasoline.

items.example: The car needs more petrol.
items.note: British English petrol corresponds to American English gasoline or gas.

items.example: Can you give me a lift to the station?
items.note: You let someone travel in your car. American English often uses give someone a ride.

items.pt: pegar um táxi; ir de táxi
items.example: Take a taxi if the bus is too slow.
items.note: Common when giving travel directions: take + a form of public transport.

items.pt: pegar um ônibus; ir de ônibus
items.example: Take a bus from the airport to the city centre.
items.note: The exercise uses take to introduce stages of a journey.

items.pt: pegar um trem; ir de trem
items.example: Take a train to the next town and get off at the second stop.
items.note: A transport instruction used in exercise 32.3. A similar expression is take the train.

learningObjectives: Identify the transport shown in the illustrations and describe journeys with by, take and ride when appropriate.
Understand map, timetable, luggage, customs, passport and tickets, including single and return tickets.
Ask about and arrange travel using book or reserve a seat in advance.
Describe train arrivals and departures using platform, arrive, depart, leave, change trains and direct train.
Describe flying using check in, online check-in, boarding card, get on, take off, land and go through customs.
Use hire a car, fill up with petrol and give someone a lift appropriately.
Avoid the source's common mistakes concerning journey versus travel and check versus control a passport; distinguish hire from buy.
Give directions using take a bus or train or taxi, get off and references to stops and stations.
